issues.issue: Preserving "any other remedy available at law or in equity" cannot be squared with the preceding sentences of Section 10, which confine Buyer to specific performance or actual damages and cap Seller's recovery at $50,000 in liquidated damages. Whether the enumerated remedies are exclusive is squarely in doubt.

Placing risk of loss on Seller until delivery of the deed conflicts with Section 6, in which Buyer accepts the Property in its condition at closing with all faults "whether now or hereafter existing." Both cannot govern loss occurring between signing and closing.

"Injury beyond the ordinary wear and tear" and "an appropriate deduction from the purchase price" supply no measure of either the triggering damage or the price adjustment, and the choice between repair and deduction is unallocated. Neither party's entitlement on a casualty is ascertainable.

"Substantial portion" is defined circularly as a portion that "would impair or otherwise affect the intended use of the Real Property" — "affect" has no threshold and "Real Property" is not the defined term "Property." Whether a given taking triggers the termination right turns on undefined words.

The ten-day period runs from Buyer's "receipt... of written notification of any such condemnation," but the clause does not say who must give that notification or make Seller's notice a condition of waiver. Whether the right to terminate can be waived absent notice from Seller is open.

"Insubstantial" is defined by the same circular test — a portion that "would not impair or otherwise affect the intended use of the Property" — with no threshold for "affect," so a taking could satisfy neither definition or arguably both. The line between the substantial and insubstantial branches is unascertainable.

The inspection right is granted "during the period of this Option including any extension periods," but this instrument is a purchase and sale agreement with no Option period of its own, and under Section 2 of the Option that period ends on exercise. When Buyer's entry right begins and ends has no referent in this Agreement.

The clause imposes duties on "Optionee" and rights on "Optionor," terms this Agreement never defines — its parties are "Seller" and "Buyer." Who must require the insurance and whose acceptance measures it is unstated in this instrument's own vocabulary.

"Said parties" has no clear antecedent in a provision that has just referred to representatives, agents and "offerors participating in the lease procurement process," and the clause imposes no obligation on Buyer itself for its invitees' damage. Who bears the restoration duty is uncertain.

The notice duty is placed on "Optionee" and owed to "Optionor," neither of which is a defined party to this Agreement, and "reasonable notice" fixes no period. The obligation cannot be applied to Buyer and Seller without construction.

The address block for notices "If to Buyer" is left blank, so no notice can be validly addressed to Buyer under the clause's own terms. The "With copy to" GSA line also appears under the Seller heading, leaving unclear whose notices must be copied to the Government.

The deemed-receipt rule supplies dates only for mail and overnight courier, omitting personal delivery, which the preceding sentence expressly authorizes as method (ii). When a personally delivered notice is effective is left unstated.

The representation is that no commission is payable "to any other person or entity for brokerage or similar services performed hereunder," which is limited to services under this Agreement and says nothing about brokers engaged in connection with the Option or the underlying transaction. The scope of "performed hereunder" is arguable.

Making time of the essence "throughout the term of this Agreement" is hard to reconcile with Section 8(a), which fixes Closing only on "a mutually agreeable date," and with the blank execution date from which the ninety-day outside date runs. Which dates are strict cannot be settled from this clause alone.

"Legal holiday" is not defined, and this transaction involves a Michigan property, an Illinois-based federal agency and a federal Buyer's assignee, so federal and state holiday calendars may differ. Which calendar extends a performance date is unspecified.

Choosing the law of the state where the Property is located cannot be squared with Section 19 of the Option, which subjects the transaction to the Contract Disputes Act and federal dispute resolution, the Buyer being GSA's assignee. Whether Michigan law or federal law governs disputes is contestable.

The Agreement binds "permitted assigns" although it contains no assignment provision defining what an assignment is or how consent is given. What makes an assign "permitted" is unstated in this instrument.

A prevailing-party fee-shifting clause is difficult to square with Section 19 of the Option, which channels disputes into the Contract Disputes Act against the United States, where such fees are not ordinarily recoverable by contract. Whether the clause is enforceable in that forum is open.

This clause requires amendments to be "in writing and executed by each party hereto," while Section 24 requires execution by the Buyer, Seller and the Government acting by GSA. The two amendment formalities cannot both be satisfied by the same instrument.

Survival runs "until fulfilled, up to and including the time of completion of any improvements to be built thereon and the written acceptance of occupancy of such improvements" by GSA — events this Agreement neither requires nor schedules, and which may never occur. The end of the survival period is indeterminate.

The clause says this Agreement "cancels and supersedes all prior agreements" while in the same breath preserving the August 2006 Real Estate Option Agreement — itself a prior agreement — as one of the only two agreements between the parties. Whether the Option survives this Agreement, and which controls in conflict, cannot be told from the words used.

Section 18 of the Option names the Option, Exhibit 1 and the recorded Memorandum of Option as the only agreements, while this clause names only this Agreement and the Option. Whether the Memorandum remains in force is left unresolved between the two integration clauses.

Disclaiming all representations "other than those expressly contained herein" is in tension with the preceding sentence, which makes the Option part of the parties' embodied agreement and preserves its representations. Whether Seller's Option representations survive the disclaimer is the question.

Amendment is conditioned on execution by "the Government, acting by GSA," which is not a signatory to this Agreement — the signature blocks provide only for Seller and Buyer. Whether a non-party's signature can be a condition of amendment, and whose it must be if the Option has been assigned, requires construction.

The bar on recording this Agreement or "any memorandum or short form hereof" sits against the Memorandum of Real Estate Option Agreement, Exhibit 3 to the Option, which was executed expressly for recording to give notice of the right to purchase. Whether that recorded memorandum offends this prohibition is arguable.

This utility statement adds gas and drops the "for its current use" qualifier that limits the identical representation in Section 7(c). Whether the utilities are warranted adequate for the contemplated federal facility or only for current use turns on which version governs.

Making utility terminations and relocations "the sole responsibility of Buyer" cannot be squared with Section 12 of the Option, under which Optionor is responsible at its own expense for the governmental approvals covering street vacations and utility relocation. Who bears relocation cost and effort is unresolved between the instruments.

Seller's duty is only to "cooperate" in securing Brownfield Plan approval, while Section 12 of the Option obliges Optionor affirmatively to draft the Brownfield Plan, submit it, and obtain approval by a fixed date. Whether Seller owes a duty of result or only of cooperation depends on which controls.

This sentence duplicates the closing sentence of Section 2 but conditions the Buyer's entitlement on repayment of the Outstanding Balance "less any setoff" rather than "less any deductions." Whether "setoff" and "deductions" mean the same reductions, and which text governs, is left to construction.
